The capital city of France is Paris.
- The French government designates Napoleon Bonaparte as its representative in charge of matters relating to foreign and colonial affairs for the time being stretching from 1802 until his death on April 6th, 1905 (the end of the First French Republic).
- It was initiated under orders of Emperor Napoleon III's ministry; it would be called "French Foreign Minister" or simply "Napoléon". In fact there were several names proposed: Châtelet-Terreau, Dantès-Bouquet de Nemours, Borzoi Napoléon I (now known as "D'Orsay"), etc., but these ideas did not win out at first because they lacked political relevance. Finally, Pompadour’s name became popular again during this period when he took part in state parties devoted exclusively to foreign policy instead of conferring with governments like Adolphe Thiers. He even arrived in Paris himself in May 1844 after an invitation sent by Tsar Alexander II, who had been ordered by Prime Minister Charles Giscard d’Estaing to make demonstrations against the Napoleonic Code adopted that year.
- Since then, neither the Leclerc nor De Gaulle have held any office other than military officer rank. However, two people, Édouard Barbet and Cardinal Georges Bovary have served as the ambassadors respectively representing Germany and Belgium within international organizations such as NATO after their ejection from the Alliance Françoise of 1703/04 due to their personal allegiances to either Austria-Hungary or Russia.

Thus, based on historical records, Paris holds the position of capital of France throughout history. Over time, as both cities underwent rapid development through industrialization, so too has Paris become the dominant urban center serving millions of residents living around its periphery today, becoming one of Europe"s most important cultural centers where art and architecture can still see significant influence across centuries past.
